title: Assembly, Fastening & DFA
description: Assembly review covering DFA principles, assembly sequence, threaded fasteners, snap fits, adhesives, permanent joints, cables, labeling, serviceability, high-volume assembly and mechanism retention.

items.text: Every separate part has a reason to exist: it moves relative to its neighbors, must be a different material, or must come apart for service
items.hint: Run a Boothroyd-Dewhurst style minimum-part-count test on the BOM. Parts that fail all three criteria are candidates for consolidation.

items.text: Part consolidation opportunities have been reviewed and the decisions recorded
items.hint: List candidate merges (brackets into housings, separate clips into snaps, multi-piece covers) with the tooling cost and risk trade-off. Unreviewed consolidation is the usual source of avoidable assembly labor.

items.text: The product assembles predominantly from one direction (top-down / Z-axis) onto a stable base part
items.hint: Step through the assembly in CAD and count reorientations of the work in process. Each flip adds handling time and a chance to drop or misalign parts.

items.text: Each part locates itself on its mating part before fastening (pins, bosses, ribs or lead-ins), with no reliance on the operator holding alignment
items.hint: Check that the part is constrained in its final position before the first screw goes in. Parts that float until clamped end up assembled out of position.

items.text: Mating features have lead-ins (chamfers or radii) so parts guide into place
items.hint: Look for square-edged pins, holes and slots that must be aligned by eye. Rule of thumb: lead-ins of about 0.5 mm (19.7 mil) or more on insertion features, sized to the expected misalignment.

items.text: Parts that look similar but are not interchangeable cannot be fitted in the wrong position or orientation (poka-yoke)
items.hint: Try to assemble every part rotated 180° or swapped with its look-alike in CAD. Add a keying feature, asymmetric pin pattern or interference so the wrong assembly physically will not go together.

items.text: Parts are either fully symmetric about their insertion axis or obviously asymmetric
items.hint: Slightly asymmetric parts are the ones that get installed backward. Exaggerate the asymmetry or make the part symmetric so orientation stops mattering.

items.text: Every fastener and joint has clear access for the specified tool, driver bit and hand during assembly
items.hint: Sweep a driver and bit envelope (and a socket, if used) along each fastener axis in CAD with the neighboring parts in place. Check finger and hand clearance for connectors and clips too.

items.text: Loose parts do not tangle, nest or stick together when handled or fed in bulk
items.hint: Open springs, thin clips, and cups or covers that stack tightly cause line jams and miscounts. Close spring ends, add anti-nesting ribs, or specify tray packaging.

items.text: Flexible, fragile or small parts are minimized, and those that remain have a defined handling method
items.hint: Tiny or delicate parts (thin films, small springs, sub-M2 screws) need tweezers, fixtures or vision. Note how each will be picked and placed.

items.text: Assembly does not depend on adjustment, shimming or selective fitting to meet its requirements
items.hint: Adjustments add time, operator skill and a failure mode. If one is unavoidable, it has a documented procedure, a defined range and a lock after setting.

items.text: The assembly sequence is documented step by step and matches the CAD assembly structure
items.hint: Produce an exploded sequence or assembly-step list and walk it through in CAD. Gaps in the sequence show up as parts that cannot be installed after their neighbors.

items.text: No part in the sequence is trapped or blocked by a part installed earlier
items.hint: Animate or step through the assembly in CAD with collision detection on. A blocked part found at the first build costs a tool change or a redesigned sequence.

items.text: Sub-assemblies can be built and functionally tested on their own before final assembly
items.hint: Group parts so that, for example, the PCBA with display or the drive train can be tested before closing the housing. Finding a defect after final assembly multiplies rework cost.

items.text: Required assembly fixtures, nests and jigs are identified and listed with their purpose
items.hint: List each fixture with the step it supports and its datum scheme. Fixtures are long-lead items and need to reference the same datums as the drawings.

items.text: Sub-assemblies are stable and do not fall apart when handled or moved between stations
items.hint: An unfastened stack held together only by gravity will come apart on the line. Add a temporary snap, a first screw or a carrier.

items.text: The assembly can be disassembled for rework without damaging parts that must be reused
items.hint: Walk through disassembly in reverse. Permanent joints (welds, adhesive, one-way snaps) on high-value parts should be deliberate decisions, not accidents.

items.text: Critical assembly steps (torque, alignment, bonding, sealing) have an in-process check defined
items.hint: Each critical step names how it is verified on the line: torque-monitored driver, go/no-go gauge, vision or functional test.

items.text: Assembly stack-ups that drive fit or function have been checked across the full tolerance range
items.hint: Confirm the assembly analysis exists for gaps, preload and clearances at worst-case and statistical limits. Cross-reference the Tolerancing & GD&T checklist for the analysis itself.

items.text: The number of different fastener sizes, lengths and head styles across the product is minimized
items.hint: Tabulate all fasteners from the BOM. Each unique screw is another bit change, feeder, part number and chance of using the wrong one.

items.text: Fasteners are metric (ISO) sizes unless a documented reason requires otherwise
items.hint: Mixing inch and metric fasteners in one product invites cross-threading and wrong-part errors in assembly and service.

items.text: Look-alike screws of different lengths are not used in the same assembly where a wrong choice causes damage
items.hint: A screw 2 mm (79 mil) too long can punch through a cosmetic wall or a battery cell. Use a distinct diameter or head, or make every location take the same screw.

items.text: Thread engagement length suits the internal thread material
items.hint: Check engagement against the material and fastener grade so the bolt breaks before the threads strip. Rule of thumb: about 1×d in steel, 1.5×d in cast iron or brass, 2×d or more in aluminum; confirm with a calculation for loaded joints.

items.text: Thread-forming screws in plastic have a drive torque and strip torque with an adequate margin between them, and the assembly torque sits inside it
items.hint: Measure drive and strip torque on molded bosses at the extremes of hole size. Rule of thumb: strip-to-drive ratio of about 3:1 or more for reliable powered driving.

items.text: Every structural joint has a specified torque derived from the required clamp load
items.hint: The torque spec should trace to a clamp-load requirement and a friction (nut factor) assumption, with joint material bearing stress checked. A torque copied from a generic chart is not a design.

items.text: Joints subject to vibration or thermal cycling have a defined anti-loosening method
items.hint: Choose from preload with adequate grip length, thread-locker, prevailing-torque nuts or locking features. Split lock washers alone are not a reliable anti-loosening method.

items.text: Thread-locker grade, application zone and cure time are specified where thread-locker is used
items.hint: Check compatibility with plastics: some anaerobic thread-lockers cause stress cracking in polycarbonate and similar plastics. Note whether the joint must be removable for service.

items.text: Fastener heads and nuts bearing on soft materials (plastics, soft aluminum, painted surfaces) use washers or flange heads sized to keep bearing stress acceptable
items.hint: Compare under-head bearing stress to the material's compressive or creep limit per datasheet. Plastic under a small screw head creeps and loses preload.

items.text: Fastener and mating materials are galvanically compatible for the environment, or the joint is isolated
items.hint: Check the anodic index difference of the pair (e.g. stainless screw in aluminum, steel in magnesium). In wet or salty service use coatings, isolating washers or a compatible fastener.

items.text: Captive screws or retention features are used wherever a dropped screw could fall into electronics or be lost in service
items.hint: Service panels and lids opened by users or field technicians should keep their screws. A loose screw inside a powered product can short a board.

items.text: Threaded inserts (heat-set, ultrasonic, press-in or molded-in) have pull-out and torque-out values that exceed the joint loads with margin
items.hint: Get pull-out and torque-out from the insert supplier for the specific plastic, then verify on molded parts. Inserts in glass-filled or thin bosses can crack the boss during installation.

items.text: Self-tapping screws into sheet metal have the correct pilot hole and enough material thickness or an extruded hole for thread engagement
items.hint: Thin sheet gives one or two threads; use an extruded (flanged) hole, clinch nut or a thicker gauge. Check the pilot hole against the screw supplier's table.

items.text: Clinch nuts, studs and standoffs in sheet metal suit the sheet thickness, hardness and edge distance per the hardware supplier
items.hint: Verify minimum sheet thickness, hole size, distance to bends and edges, and that the sheet is softer than the hardware. Wrong hardness means the fastener spins out.

items.text: Screw lengths leave clearance at the bottom of blind holes and bosses
items.hint: A screw that bottoms out reaches torque without clamping. Check the stack in CAD at maximum screw length and minimum hole depth.

items.text: Every snap fit has its assembly (insertion) force calculated or measured and within the operator or machine limit
items.hint: Calculate from beam deflection, lead-in angle and friction, or measure on prototypes. High insertion forces cause operator fatigue and incomplete engagement.

items.text: Every snap fit has a retention force that meets the requirement, including drop and handling loads
items.hint: Calculate or test retention force at the return angle; a 90° return is usually permanent. Check retention after the snap has aged at maximum temperature.

items.text: Snap fit strain during assembly stays below the material's allowable strain per datasheet, including at worst-case tolerance
items.hint: Use the maximum interference from the tolerance stack, not nominal. Reduce allowable strain for glass-filled grades and for snaps assembled more than once.

items.text: Snaps that must release for service have a defined release method that does not require breaking parts
items.hint: Provide a release slot, a tool access point or a ramped return. Show the service tool and its access in CAD.

items.text: Snaps designed to be reused are rated for the required number of assembly cycles
items.hint: Allowable strain for repeated cycles is lower than for one-time assembly. Cycle-test prototypes in the production material.

items.text: Snap fits do not stay deflected (preloaded) in the assembled state unless the material creep has been accounted for
items.hint: A snap held under strain relaxes over time, especially at elevated temperature. Design for zero deflection once seated or check creep data per datasheet.

items.text: Engagement of each snap can be confirmed by the assembler (audible click, visual flush, or a check feature)
items.hint: A half-engaged snap passes assembly and fails in the field. Add a flush indicator or a gap that is visible only when not seated.

items.text: Metal spring clips and retaining rings have groove dimensions and installation tools specified per the supplier
items.hint: Check groove diameter, width and edge radius against the supplier catalog, and that the installation tool fits in the space available.

items.text: The adhesive or tape is qualified for the surface energy of both substrates
items.hint: Low-surface-energy plastics (PP, PE, POM, some TPEs, silicone) need a specific adhesive, primer or surface treatment. Check the adhesive supplier's substrate compatibility data.

items.text: Surface preparation (cleaning, abrading, plasma, flame or primer) is specified and practical on the production line
items.hint: Bond strength depends more on surface prep than on the adhesive. Specify the solvent or treatment, the time window to bonding, and how it is verified (e.g. dyne pens).

items.text: Mold release agents and contamination from upstream processes are controlled on bonded surfaces
items.hint: Silicone release agents and finger oils kill adhesion. Agree release-agent-free molding or a cleaning step with the molder for bonded parts.

items.text: Liquid adhesive bond line thickness is controlled by design (stand-offs, beads or spacer features)
items.hint: Without a controlled gap the bond line varies from starved to thick. Use the adhesive supplier's recommended bond line range and add features to set it.

items.text: Adhesive cure time, temperature and fixture time fit the production cycle, and handling strength is reached before the next step
items.hint: Check the supplier's cure profile. Moving parts before handling strength causes misaligned or weakened bonds.

items.text: Pressure-sensitive adhesive joints have specified application pressure and dwell time
items.hint: PSA strength builds with pressure and time. Specify roller or press pressure and dwell, and the time before load is applied, per the tape supplier.

items.text: Adhesive and tape are rated for the full operating and storage temperature range, humidity and chemical exposure
items.hint: Compare service temperature, humidity and cleaning agents against the supplier data. PSAs soften and creep at elevated temperature.

items.text: Bonded joints are loaded in shear or compression, not peel or cleavage
items.hint: Adhesive peel strength is a small fraction of its shear strength. Add geometry so the load path avoids peel at bond edges.

items.text: Adhesive or tape geometry (die-cut shape, bead path) is fully defined on a drawing
items.hint: Die-cut tape needs a drawing with liner tabs and tolerances; dispensed beads need path, bead size and start/stop points.

items.text: Bonded parts can be reworked or serviced where required, or the joint is intentionally permanent
items.hint: Decide whether the bond must be separable (pull-tab adhesive strips, heat-release tape) and document the decision.

items.text: Adhesive outgassing, corrosivity and compatibility with nearby electronics and optics are checked
items.hint: Acetoxy-cure silicones release acetic acid that corrodes copper; some adhesives fog lenses. Use neutral-cure or low-outgassing grades near electronics or optics.

items.text: Ultrasonic weld joints use a joint design (energy director, shear joint) suited to the plastic and the welding supplier's recommendations
items.hint: Amorphous plastics weld well with energy directors; semi-crystalline plastics usually need shear joints. Review the joint with the welding equipment supplier before tool release.

items.text: Ultrasonic or other plastic weld joints have flash traps or are hidden where flash would be visible or interfere
items.hint: Weld flash on cosmetic or sealing surfaces is a frequent first-article rejection. Add flash traps or move the joint.

items.text: Ultrasonically welded assemblies keep sensitive components away from horn energy or have been tested for damage
items.hint: Ultrasonic energy can crack crystal oscillators, MEMS sensors and solder joints. Test welded PCBAs functionally after welding.

items.text: Heat-stake and cold-stake boss geometry follows the staking equipment supplier's guide for boss diameter, height and head form
items.hint: Check that boss height leaves enough material to form the head and that the head clamps the part without cracking. Verify pull-off strength on samples.

items.text: Rivet grip range matches the actual material stack, and hole sizes and edge distances follow the rivet supplier's guide
items.hint: Check the stack at minimum and maximum tolerance. Blind rivets into plastics or thin sheet may need a large-flange or soft-set style.

items.text: Press-fit interference, assembly force and retention force have been calculated across the tolerance range
items.hint: Compute hoop stress at maximum interference and retention at minimum interference. Check the press force against the available press and the part's strength.

items.text: Press fits into plastic account for creep and stress relaxation over the product life and temperature range
items.hint: Plastic hubs relax and lose retention, especially when hot. Use knurls, ribs (crush ribs) or a metal insert, and check against creep data per datasheet.

items.text: Pressed and welded joints have a pass/fail criterion that can be checked in production (force-displacement window, weld depth, or pull test)
items.hint: Monitor press force or displacement or weld collapse on the line. An unmonitored permanent joint cannot be screened for bad parts.

items.text: Every cable and harness has a defined route in CAD with its retention points modeled
items.hint: Model cables at real diameter and minimum bend radius. A cable left out of CAD ends up pinched or forced into space that does not exist.

items.text: Cable bend radius stays at or above the cable or FPC supplier's minimum at every bend, including dynamic bends
items.hint: Check flex and FPC bends against the supplier's static and dynamic bend radius. FPCs that flex in use need a dynamic-rated construction.

items.text: Cables cannot be pinched between mating housings, fasteners or moving parts during assembly or in use
items.hint: Check closing gaps and screw paths along the cable route. Pinched cables fail intermittently and are a common field return.

items.text: Cables are retained so they cannot migrate onto hot, sharp or moving parts
items.hint: Use clips, guides, tape or tie points. Check sheet-metal edges along the route are deburred or protected with grommets.

items.text: Strain relief is provided so that pulls on external cables do not load solder joints, crimps or connectors
items.hint: Pull on the external cable in the design review and trace the load path. It should end in the housing, not at the PCB.

items.text: Connectors can be mated and unmated with the required hand or tool access in the assembly sequence
items.hint: Check that board-to-board and cable connectors can be seated with a straight push and inspected, and that latches can be released for service.

items.text: Connector mating is verifiable (latch click, full-seat feature or test) and cannot be mis-mated with a similar connector nearby
items.hint: Use different keying, pin counts or colors for adjacent identical connectors. A partly seated connector passes initial test and fails after shipping.

items.text: Cable lengths have slack for assembly and service but not so much excess that it must be stuffed into the housing
items.hint: Check the cable length with the housing open in the service position and closed. Excess loops press on components and block air flow.

items.text: Grounding connections to the chassis (bonding straps, ring terminals, grounding screws) have a defined assembly step and contact method
items.hint: Specify star washers, thread-cutting screws or clean contact areas so the bond is made reliably. Coordinate the electrical requirement with EE.

items.text: Wire and cable insulation is protected where it passes through holes or over edges
items.hint: Grommets, edge trim or rolled edges on every pass-through. Bare sheet-metal edges cut insulation under vibration.

items.text: Every required label has a defined location, size and flat area that is accessible after assembly
items.hint: Place the rating label, serial number and regulatory marks on a flat, unobstructed surface. Check visibility in the installed orientation.

items.text: Label materials and adhesives suit the substrate and the environment for the product life
items.hint: Check abrasion, cleaning agents, UV and temperature against the label supplier's data. Regulatory labels must remain legible for the product life.

items.text: Parts that look alike carry an identifying mark (part number, cavity number, material code) molded or marked in a non-cosmetic area
items.hint: Part and material identification supports traceability and recycling. Include cavity identification for multi-cavity molds.

items.text: Traceability marking (serial, date code or lot) is defined for parts and sub-assemblies that require it
items.hint: Define what is marked, by what method (laser, label, mold date wheel) and where it is recorded. Medical and regulated products usually require this.

items.text: Assembly orientation aids (arrows, alignment marks, color codes) are added where orientation is not obvious
items.hint: Use these in addition to poka-yoke features, not as a substitute for them.

items.text: Parts expected to fail or wear can be reached and replaced without disassembling unrelated parts
items.hint: Rank parts by expected failure rate and count the steps to replace each. High-failure parts behind many others drive service cost.

items.text: Consumable parts (filters, seals, batteries, brushes, blades) are replaceable by the intended user or technician with the intended tools
items.hint: Check the replacement procedure against the user profile: no special tools for end users, defined tools for technicians.

items.text: Whether the battery is user-replaceable, service-replaceable or not replaceable is a deliberate decision consistent with regulations in the target markets
items.hint: Some markets require user-removable or replaceable portable batteries. Confirm the requirement with regulatory and record the decision.

items.text: Battery disconnection or removal is possible before other service work where stored energy creates a hazard
items.hint: Service steps should isolate the battery early. Check that the connector or tabs can be reached without passing tools across live conductors.

items.text: Service access does not require breaking seals, cosmetic parts or permanent joints that cannot be restored
items.hint: If opening the product destroys a gasket, label or adhesive bond, the service kit and procedure must include its replacement.

items.text: Fasteners used for service access are standard drives that the service organization has, or the special drive is a deliberate tamper-resistance decision
items.hint: Security drives deter users but must be in the service toolkit. Record the decision.

items.text: Service-replaceable parts are keyed or identified so that the correct part is fitted after repair
items.hint: Field technicians lack factory fixtures and work instructions. Keying and clear marking prevent wrong-part or wrong-orientation repairs.

items.text: Assembly time is estimated for each step and the total meets the cost target
items.hint: Use a DFA time estimate or line study per step. Compare the total against the labor cost assumption in the business case.

items.text: Parts intended for automated feeding or pick-and-place have consistent orientation features and gripper surfaces
items.hint: Confirm with the automation integrator that each part can be fed (bowl, tray, tape) and gripped. Flat, featureless or tangled parts block automation.

items.text: Fasteners intended for automatic feeding are compatible with the feeder (head geometry, length-to-head ratio)
items.hint: Short screws with large heads, or very small screws, may not feed reliably. Confirm with the feeder supplier.

items.text: Parts are packaged and delivered to the line in an orientation that avoids extra handling
items.hint: Specify trays, tape or kits for parts that are damaged or slow to orient from bulk. Include packaging in the supplier quotation.

items.text: Station count and line balance are planned so that no single step limits throughput
items.hint: Identify the longest step (often cure, test or welding) and plan parallel stations or a different method.

items.text: End-of-line test coverage is defined for the functions the assembly process can affect
items.hint: List the assembly-induced failure modes (missed fastener, unseated connector, leak) and map each to a test that detects it.

items.text: Bearings and bushings are axially and radially retained in their housings by a defined method (shoulder, retaining ring, press fit or adhesive)
items.hint: Check that axial loads in both directions have a path to the housing. Bearings retained only by friction walk out under load or thermal cycling.

items.text: Bearing and bushing fits on shafts and housings follow the bearing supplier's recommended fit for the load case
items.hint: Rotating inner ring loads usually need interference on the shaft; check the supplier's table. Wrong fits cause creep, fretting or lost clearance.

items.text: Lubricant type and quantity are specified for every lubricated interface and are compatible with the adjacent plastics and elastomers
items.hint: Some greases and oils swell elastomers or stress-crack plastics. Specify the grease by product name, amount and application area.

items.text: Lubricant application is a controlled step (dispensed amount, location) in the assembly sequence
items.hint: Hand-applied grease varies widely. Specify the dispensing method and how the amount is verified.

items.text: Shaft end-play and axial position are controlled by design within a specified range
items.hint: Check the axial stack across tolerance. Too little end-play binds when hot; too much causes noise and gear misalignment.

items.text: Springs are captive so they cannot escape during assembly, service or failure
items.hint: Use spring seats, posts or pockets. A loose spring is a launch hazard during service and a lost part on the line.

items.text: Springs are preloaded during assembly in a way that does not require the operator to hold them compressed
items.hint: Use a fixture, a ramp or an assembly order that compresses the spring as parts close. Operators holding springs leads to slips and injuries.

items.text: Hinge pins, pivots and slides have defined retention and wear surfaces suited to the required cycle life
items.hint: Check retention of the pin (head, ring, stake) and the wear pair materials. Cross-reference the validation plan for cycle testing.

items.text: Moving parts have clearance to adjacent parts and cables through their full range of motion
items.hint: Run a motion study or check interference at the travel extremes, including tolerances and part deflection under load.
